claim: Defensive system activation promotes heightened perception of threat signals.
source: Defensive system activation promotes heightened perception of threat signals, and excessive attention to threat signals has been discussed as a contributory factor in the etiology of anxiety disorders.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data from this study.

claim: Excessive attention to threat signals has been discussed as a contributory factor in the etiology of anxiety disorders.
source: Defensive system activation promotes heightened perception of threat signals, and excessive attention to threat signals has been discussed as a contributory factor in the etiology of anxiety disorders.
evidence: This references existing literature and discussion in the field.

claim: 67 healthy participants underwent differential fear conditioning followed by a generalization test.
source: To test the hypothesis that social fear generalization prompts sharpened tuning in the visuocortical representation of social threat cues, 67 healthy participants underwent differential fear conditioning, followed by a generalization test in which participants viewed faces varying in similarity with the threat-associated face.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample size of the study.

claim: Generalization of social threat sharpens visuocortical tuning of social threat cues.
source: We found that generalization of social threat sharpens visuocortical tuning of social threat cues, whereas ratings of fearfulness showed generalization, linearly decreasing with decreasing similarity to the threat-associated face.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Ratings of fearfulness showed generalization, linearly decreasing with decreasing similarity to the threat-associated face.
source: We found that generalization of social threat sharpens visuocortical tuning of social threat cues, whereas ratings of fearfulness showed generalization, linearly decreasing with decreasing similarity to the threat-associated face.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Individuals who reported greater anxiety in social situations showed heightened sharpened tuning of visuocortical neurons to facial identity cues.
source: Moreover, individuals who reported greater anxiety in social situations also showed heightened sharpened tuning of visuocortical neurons to facial identity cues, indicating the behavioral relevance of visuocortical tuning during generalization learning.
evidence: This is a finding from the study correlating social anxiety with visuocortical tuning.

claim: The dysregulation of selective perception and differential responding to threat versus safety cues is at the core of many psychiatric problems.
source: The dysregulation of these functions is at the core of many psychiatric problems.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The process of overgeneralization has been of particular interest in anxiety disorder research.
source: Given its intuitive relation with exaggerated fear and anxiety, the process of overgeneralization—showing threat responses to safety cues that resemble threat-associated stimuli—has been of particular interest.
evidence: This describes the research focus in the field.

claim: Previous clinical and translational work on fear generalization has yielded contradictory findings.
source: However, previous clinical and translational work has yielded contradictory findings.
evidence: This summarizes the state of the literature.

claim: Some authors observed overgeneralization in patients with anxiety disorders.
source: While some authors observed overgeneralization in patients with anxiety disorders (Kaczkurkin et al., 2017; Lissek et al., 2014b; Lissek et al., 2010), others did not (Ahrens et al., 2016; Tinoco-González et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some authors did not observe overgeneralization in patients with anxiety disorders.
source: While some authors observed overgeneralization in patients with anxiety disorders (Kaczkurkin et al., 2017; Lissek et al., 2014b; Lissek et al., 2010), others did not (Ahrens et al., 2016; Tinoco-González et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Different physiological systems respond differently to varying similarity with a fear stimulus.
source: This lack of convergent findings may be due to the fact that different physiological systems respond differently to varying similarity with a fear stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn to explain contradictory findings in the literature.

claim: Defensive engagement is indexed by somato-visceral measures such as fear-potentiated startle, skin conductance, and cardiovascular responses.
source: This defensive engagement is indexed by somato-visceral measures, such as fear-potentiated startle, skin conductance, and cardiovascular responses (Boecker and Pauli, 2019; Bradley and Lang, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Defensive mobilization includes heightened sensory processing, that is, perception and attention to threat.
source: In addition to preparing autonomic and motor efferent systems for action, defensive mobilization also includes heightened sensory processing, that is, perception and attention to threat (Robinson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Stimuli predicting threat are attended more than neutral cues.
source: In line with this notion, a substantial body of research has shown that stimuli predicting threat are attended more than neutral cues, and that heightened attention toward threatening stimuli is pronounced in patients with anxiety disorders (Bar-Haim et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Heightened attention toward threatening stimuli is pronounced in patients with anxiety disorders.
source: In line with this notion, a substantial body of research has shown that stimuli predicting threat are attended more than neutral cues, and that heightened attention toward threatening stimuli is pronounced in patients with anxiety disorders (Bar-Haim et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Excessive attention to threatening stimuli has been discussed as causal or contributory in the etiology of anxiety disorders.
source: As a consequence, excessive attention to threatening stimuli has been discussed as causal or contributory in the etiology of anxiety disorders (Clark and Wells, 1995; Rapee and Heimberg, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Direct neurophysiological evidence of heightened attention to threat in clinical disorders is scarce.
source: Direct neurophysiological evidence of heightened attention to threat in clinical disorders is scarce, however, and findings of both heightened and diminished attention have been reported.
evidence: This summarizes the state of the literature.

claim: The ssVEP is an oscillatory neuronal response to stimuli that are periodically modulated in luminance.
source: The ssVEP is an oscillatory neuronal response to stimuli that are periodically modulated in luminance.
evidence: This is a definition based on established knowledge.

claim: Heightened ssVEP amplitudes mark increased visuocortical activation and can be used to index attentional processes.
source: Heightened ssVEP amplitudes mark increased visuocortical activation and can be used to index attentional processes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ssVEP measure.

claim: Attended features facilitate visuocortical activation compared to unattended features.
source: For example, attended features (Müller et al., 2006) and selective spatial attention (Müller et al., 1998) facilitate visuocortical activation compared to unattended features and locations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Selective spatial attention facilitates visuocortical activation compared to unattended locations.
source: For example, attended features (Müller et al., 2006) and selective spatial attention (Müller et al., 1998) facilitate visuocortical activation compared to unattended features and locations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SsVEPs show increased amplitudes for emotional compared to neutral stimuli.
source: SsVEPs are also sensitive to emotional processes and show increased amplitudes for emotional compared to neutral stimuli (Keil et al., 2003; Kemp et al., 2002; McTeague et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The amplitude of the ssVEP differentiates threat from safety signals, being selectively heightened for conditioned threat cues.
source: The amplitude of the ssVEP differentiates threat from safety signals, being selectively heightened for conditioned threat cues (reviewed in Miskovic and Keil, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review.

claim: McTeague et al., 2015 utilized ssVEPs to study population-level tuning of orientation-selective neurons in the primary visual cortex during fear generalization.
source: Building on these findings, McTeague et al., 2015 utilized ssVEPs to study population-level tuning of orientation-selective neurons in the primary visual cortex during fear generalization.
evidence: This describes a previous study.

claim: After several conditioning trials, the CS+ prompted enhanced visuocortical engagement, accompanied by a suppression of the grating orientations with highest similarity to the CS+.
source: After several conditioning trials, the CS+ prompted enhanced visuocortical engagement, accompanied by a suppression of the grating orientations with highest similarity to the CS+.
evidence: This describes findings from McTeague et al., 2015.

claim: The tuning pattern observed by McTeague et al., 2015 suggests lateral inhibitory interactions among orientation-selective neuronal populations in the visual cortex.
source: This tuning pattern, which contrasts with the gradually decreasing generalization gradient observed in self-report and somato-visceral indices of learning, suggests lateral inhibitory interactions among orientation-selective neuronal populations in the visual cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from McTeague et al., 2015.

claim: There is substantial evidence for single-unit and population level tuning in face-specific areas in the human and primate brain.
source: This hypothesis is grounded in work showing substantial evidence for single-unit and population level (LFPs, fMRI) tuning in face-specific areas in the human and primate brain (Freiwald and Tsao, 2010; Freiwald et al., 2009; Gilaie-Dotan and Malach, 2007; Leopold et al., 2006; Loffler et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: There are neurons and neuronal populations in face-sensitive cortical areas that show gradual responses to varying facial identity.
source: These studies have demonstrated that there are neurons and neuronal populations in face-sensitive cortical areas, like the occipital face area (OFA) and the fusiform face area (FFA), which show gradual responses to varying facial identify, often referred to as 'tuning' to facial identities (Chang and Tsao, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: During habituation, higher social anxiety was associated with higher ssVEP-SNRs in general.
source: During habituation, the linear mixed model analysis including the within-factor CS-type (two levels: CS+ vs CS-) and social anxiety as a continuous between-variable revealed a significant main effect for social anxiety, indicating that higher social anxiety was associated with higher ssVEP-SNRs in general and a non-significant trend for CS-type (CS+: M = 3.61, SD = 1.91; CS-: M = 3.39 SD=1.77).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of the habituation phase data.

claim: During habituation, there was a non-significant trend for CS-type.
source: During habituation, the linear mixed model analysis including the within-factor CS-type (two levels: CS+ vs CS-) and social anxiety as a continuous between-variable revealed a significant main effect for social anxiety, indicating that higher social anxiety was associated with higher ssVEP-SNRs in general and a non-significant trend for CS-type (CS+: M = 3.61, SD = 1.91; CS-: M = 3.39 SD=1.77).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of the habituation phase data.

claim: During habituation, there was no CS-type x social anxiety interaction.
source: There was no CS-type x social anxiety interaction (see Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of the habituation phase data.

claim: During habituation, subjects rated the CS- as slightly more unpleasant than the CS+.
source: However, subjects rated the CS- as slightly more unpleasant than the CS+, (CS+: M = 4.60, SD = 1.22; CS-: M = 4.99 SD=1.25).
evidence: This is a finding from the valence ratings during habituation.

claim: During habituation, there was no significant effect of CS-type on arousal ratings.
source: With regard to arousal ratings, there was no significant effect for CS-type (CS+: M = 3.69, SD = 1.61; CS-: M = 3.58 SD=1.58), social anxiety, or CS-type x social anxiety interaction.
evidence: This is a finding from the arousal ratings during habituation.

claim: After acquisition, subjects reacted with higher ssVEP amplitudes to the CS+ compared to the CS-.
source: After the CS+ had been paired with the US (see Figure 2), linear mixed model analyses for ssVEPs yielded a main effect of CS-type and a small effect of social anxiety, demonstrating that subjects reacted with higher amplitudes to the CS+ (M = 3.69, SD = 1.80) compared to the CS- (M = 3.33, SD = 1.56, see Figure 3a) and that higher social anxiety was associated with higher amplitudes in general (see Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the ssVEP data during acquisition.

claim: After acquisition, higher social anxiety was associated with higher ssVEP amplitudes in general.
source: After the CS+ had been paired with the US (see Figure 2), linear mixed model analyses for ssVEPs yielded a main effect of CS-type and a small effect of social anxiety, demonstrating that subjects reacted with higher amplitudes to the CS+ (M = 3.69, SD = 1.80) compared to the CS- (M = 3.33, SD = 1.56, see Figure 3a) and that higher social anxiety was associated with higher amplitudes in general (see Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the ssVEP data during acquisition.

claim: After acquisition, there was no significant CS-type x social anxiety interaction for ssVEPs.
source: There was no significant CS-type x social anxiety interaction.
evidence: This is a finding from the ssVEP data during acquisition.

claim: After acquisition, subjects rated the CS+ as more unpleasant compared to the CS-.
source: After acquisition, there was a significant main effect of CS-type for both valence and arousal ratings (see Table 2), demonstrating that subjects rated the CS+ as more unpleasant (M = 6.42, SD = 1.41) and more arousing (M = 6.51, SD = 1.63) compared to the CS- (unpleasantness: M = 4.73, SD = 1.34; arousal: M = 3.69, SD = 1.94, see Figure 3c and d).
evidence: This is a finding from the valence ratings after acquisition.

claim: After acquisition, subjects rated the CS+ as more arousing compared to the CS-.
source: After acquisition, there was a significant main effect of CS-type for both valence and arousal ratings (see Table 2), demonstrating that subjects rated the CS+ as more unpleasant (M = 6.42, SD = 1.41) and more arousing (M = 6.51, SD = 1.63) compared to the CS- (unpleasantness: M = 4.73, SD = 1.34; arousal: M = 3.69, SD = 1.94, see Figure 3c and d).
evidence: This is a finding from the arousal ratings after acquisition.

claim: After acquisition, US expectancy ratings were higher for the CS+ compared to the CS-.
source: The analysis detected a main effect of CS-type (see Table 2), with higher US expectancy ratings for the CS+ (M = 72.09, SD = 21.71) compared to the CS- (M = 8.66, SD = 18.74), underlining that the experimental manipulation was effective (see Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a finding from the US expectancy ratings after acquisition.

claim: The experimental manipulation was effective.
source: The analysis detected a main effect of CS-type (see Table 2), with higher US expectancy ratings for the CS+ (M = 72.09, SD = 21.71) compared to the CS- (M = 8.66, SD = 18.74), underlining that the experimental manipulation was effective (see Figure 3b).
evidence: This is an inference based on the US expectancy ratings.

claim: During generalization, there was a main effect of CS-type on ssVEPs.
source: The CS-type (six levels: CS+ vs GS1 vs GS2 vs GS3 vs GS4 vs CS-) x social anxiety linear mixed model provided a main effect of CS-type and a marginal effect of social anxiety (see Figures 4 and 5a and Table 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of the generalization phase data.

claim: During generalization, there was a marginal effect of social anxiety on ssVEPs.
source: The CS-type (six levels: CS+ vs GS1 vs GS2 vs GS3 vs GS4 vs CS-) x social anxiety linear mixed model provided a main effect of CS-type and a marginal effect of social anxiety (see Figures 4 and 5a and Table 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of the generalization phase data.

claim: During generalization, post-hoc contrasts indicated significant differences between GS4 vs CS-, GS3 vs CS-, and CS+ vs CS- for ssVEPs.
source: Post-hoc contrasts indicated significant differences between GS4 vs CS-, t(325) = 2.94, p=0.003, GS3 vs CS-, t(325) = 3.24, p=0.001, and CS+ vs CS-, t(325) = 2.17, p=0.031, but not between GS2 vs CS-, t(325) = 1.75, p=0.081, and GS1 vs CS-, t(325) = 0.82, p=0.411.
evidence: This is a finding from the post-hoc analysis of the generalization phase data.

claim: During generalization, there was no stimulus type x social anxiety interaction for ssVEPs.
source: However, the omnibus-test revealed no stimulus type x social anxiety interaction.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of the generalization phase data.

claim: The main effect of weighted CS-type received support for the lateral inhibition pattern only.
source: The main effect of weighted CS-type received support for the lateral inhibition pattern only, BFLa1/0 = 13.26, but not for the quadratic, BFQ1/0 = 0.14, or linear trend, BFLi1/0 = 0.13.
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian analysis.

claim: The strongest evidence could be found for the full interaction model and the lateral inhibition pattern.
source: The strongest evidence could be found for the full interaction model (SNR ~CS type + social anxiety + CS-type x social anxiety) and the lateral inhibition pattern, BFLa3/0 = 57.32, which substantially extends the support of the main effects model, BFLa3/La2 = 3.13, suggesting that the accentuation of the lateral inhibition pattern increased with higher social anxiety.
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian analysis.

claim: The accentuation of the lateral inhibition pattern increased with higher social anxiety.
source: The strongest evidence could be found for the full interaction model (SNR ~CS type + social anxiety + CS-type x social anxiety) and the lateral inhibition pattern, BFLa3/0 = 57.32, which substantially extends the support of the main effects model, BFLa3/La2 = 3.13, suggesting that the accentuation of the lateral inhibition pattern increased with higher social anxiety.
evidence: This is an inference from the Bayesian analysis results.

claim: The lateral inhibition model is 858 times more likely than the quadratic trend model.
source: Results for the full interaction model demonstrated that the lateral inhibition model is 858 times more likely than the quadratic trend model and 502 times more likely than the linear trend model.
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian model comparison.

claim: The lateral inhibition model is 502 times more likely than the linear trend model.
source: Results for the full interaction model demonstrated that the lateral inhibition model is 858 times more likely than the quadratic trend model and 502 times more likely than the linear trend model.
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian model comparison.

claim: There is a moderate, positive correlation between social anxiety and the visuocortical tuning index.
source: The regression analysis revealed a moderate, positive correlation between social anxiety and the visuocortical tuning index, r(65) = .288, p = 0.018, BF1/0 = 3.65, confirming that the accentuation of the lateral inhibition pattern increased with higher social anxiety, while the weak correlations between social anxiety and the index for the quadratic, r(65) = .146, p = 0.238, BF2/0 = 0.52, or linear trend, r(65) = .137, p = 0.268, BF3/0 = 0.49, missed significance and did not receive support from Bayesian-analyses.
evidence: This is a finding from the regression analysis.

claim: During generalization, subjects differentiated among the CS- and the CS+ plus three GS for arousal ratings.
source: With regard to arousal (see Figure 5c), subjects differentiated among the CS- and the CS+ plus three GS: CS- versus CS+, t(325) = 14.93, p<0.001, CS- versus GS1, t(325) = 10.28, p<0.001, CS- versus GS2, t(325) = 5.24, p<0.001, and CS- versus GS3, t(325) = 3.12, p=0.002, but not CS- versus GS4, t(325) = 1.06, p=0.290.
evidence: This is a finding from the arousal ratings during generalization.

claim: During generalization, valence ratings showed differences between CS- and CS+, CS- and GS1, CS- and GS2, and CS- and GS3, but not between CS- and GS4.
source: For valence ratings (see Figure 4d), results showed differences between CS- and CS+, t(325) = 10.95, p<0.001, CS- and GS1, t(325) = 7.14, p<0.001, CS- and GS2, t(325) = 3.41, p<0.001, and CS- and GS3, t(325) = 2.06, p=0.040, but not between CS- and GS4, t(325) = .64, p=0.526.
evidence: This is a finding from the valence ratings during generalization.

claim: All subjects transferred their fear response reflected in both valence and arousal ratings from the CS+ to three GSs.
source: These results suggest that all subjects transferred their fear response reflected in both valence and arousal ratings from the CS+ to three GSs.
evidence: This is an inference from the valence and arousal ratings during generalization.

claim: During generalization, US expectancy analysis revealed a main effect of CS-type.
source: US expectancy analysis revealed a main effect of CS-type (see Figure 5b and Table 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the US expectancy ratings during generalization.

claim: During generalization, post-hoc contrasts for US expectancy yielded significant effects for the comparison of CS- versus CS+, GS1, and GS2.
source: Post-hoc contrasts yielded significant effects for the comparison of CS- versus CS+ t(325) = 13.73, p<0.001; GS1: t(325) = 8.88, p<0.001; and GS2: t(325) = 3.84, p<0.001.
evidence: This is a finding from the post-hoc analysis of US expectancy ratings during generalization.

claim: Subjects showed an enhanced tendency to generalize their conditioned fear reaction, indicated by the fact that they expected the GS1 and GS2 to be followed by the US.
source: As found in valence and arousal ratings, subjects showed an enhanced tendency to generalize their conditioned fear reaction, indicated by the fact that they expected the GS1 and GS2 to be followed by the US, although they had never been paired with the US.
evidence: This is an inference from the US expectancy ratings during generalization.

claim: The visuocortical responses did not show a monotonic generalization gradient, but instead displayed a response pattern consistent with sharpening of the threat face representation.
source: Importantly, the visuocortical responses did not show a monotonic generalization gradient, but instead displayed a response pattern consistent with sharpening of the threat face representation.
evidence: This is a summary of the ssVEP findings during generalization.

claim: The ssVEP amplitude for the CS+ was increased, but followed by an immediate reduction for the closest GS (GS1), and a slow increase in response to the remaining GSs, before it was again reduced for the learned safety cue (CS-).
source: Instead, ssVEP amplitude for the CS+ was increased, but followed by an immediate reduction for the closest GS (GS1), and a slow increase in response to the remaining GSs, before it was again reduced for the learned safety cue (CS-).
evidence: This describes the pattern of ssVEP responses during generalization.

claim: The observed ssVEP response pattern is consistent with the response pattern of orientation sensitive neurons in the visual cortex during a fear generalization paradigm.
source: This observation is consistent with the response pattern of orientation sensitive neurons in the visual cortex during a fear generalization paradigm with enhanced visuocortical engagement to the CS+ and a suppression of the grating orientations with the highest similarity to the CS+ (McTeague et al., 2015).
evidence: This compares the current findings to previous work by McTeague et al., 2015.

claim: There is a dissociation in the aversive generalization patterns of sensory compared to efferent and autonomic systems.
source: Together, these findings suggest that there is a dissociation in the aversive generalization patterns of sensory compared to efferent and autonomic systems, which is consistent with the idea that fear generalization is an active and multifaceted process that integrates a wide variety of signals to organize adaptive fear responses (Onat and Büchel, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference from the combined findings of ssVEP and rating data.

claim: Fear generalization is an active and multifaceted process that integrates a wide variety of signals to organize adaptive fear responses.
source: Together, these findings suggest that there is a dissociation in the aversive generalization patterns of sensory compared to efferent and autonomic systems, which is consistent with the idea that fear generalization is an active and multifaceted process that integrates a wide variety of signals to organize adaptive fear responses (Onat and Büchel, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Visuocortical engagement with specific stimulus features varies with the motivational relevance of these features.
source: A large body of work has shown that visuocortical engagement with specific stimulus features varies with the motivational relevance of these features (Bradley et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Threat-induced sensory changes in low-level visual areas occur independently of the conscious awareness of the CS-US contingencies.
source: Using steady-state visual evoked fields (the magnetoencephalographic counterpart of ssVEPs), two studies could demonstrate that threat-induced sensory changes in low-level visual areas occur independently of the conscious awareness of the CS-US contingencies (Moratti and Keil, 2009; Yuan et al., 2018), suggesting that visuocortical responses are to some extent independent of higher level cognitive processes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Visuocortical responses are to some extent independent of higher level cognitive processes.
source: Using steady-state visual evoked fields (the magnetoencephalographic counterpart of ssVEPs), two studies could demonstrate that threat-induced sensory changes in low-level visual areas occur independently of the conscious awareness of the CS-US contingencies (Moratti and Keil, 2009; Yuan et al., 2018), suggesting that visuocortical responses are to some extent independent of higher level cognitive processes.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited studies.

claim: Threat-induced changes in the sensory system represent short-term plasticity in the early visual cortex, which might be induced by projections from subcortical structures like the amygdala or thalamus.
source: In contrast, it has been suggested, that threat-induced changes in the sensory system represent short-term plasticity in the early visual cortex, which might be induced by projections from subcortical structures like the amygdala or thalamus (Miskovic and Keil, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Verbal reports reflect a more cognitive component of the defensive response.
source: This could be one reason for the divergence between visuocortical and subjective responses, as verbal reports reflect a more cognitive component of the defensive response (LeDoux and Pine, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: McTeague et al., 2015 found a dissociation between the visuocortical and the fear-potentiated startle responses.
source: On the other hand, McTeague et al., 2015 also found a dissociation between the visuocortical and the fear-potentiated startle responses.
evidence: This describes a finding from a previous study.

claim: The startle reflex is assumed to be directly modulated by amygdala projections.
source: The startle reflex, as an index of the autonomic component of the efferent system, is also assumed to be directly modulated by amygdala projections (Davis, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: It is most adaptive for the organism to enhance sensory specificity in the visual cortex to distinguish the motivational information-providing stimulus from other sensory signals.
source: Taking an evolutionary perspective, it is most adaptive for the organism to enhance sensory specificity in the visual cortex to distinguish the motivational information-providing stimulus from others sensory signals as reflected in the lateral inhibition model.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation from an evolutionary perspective.

claim: The 'efferent' readiness to respond to a potential threat is generalized, as reflected in a monotonically decreasing generalization gradient.
source: On the other hand, the 'efferent' readiness to respond to a potential threat is generalized, as reflected in a monotonically decreasing generalization gradient, because a false alarm is less costly than a - potentially fatal - miss.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation from an evolutionary perspective.

claim: A false alarm is less costly than a potentially fatal miss.
source: On the other hand, the 'efferent' readiness to respond to a potential threat is generalized, as reflected in a monotonically decreasing generalization gradient, because a false alarm is less costly than a - potentially fatal - miss.
evidence: This is a speculative reasoning from an evolutionary perspective.

claim: McTeague et al., 2015 explained their finding of visuocortical sharpening as a consequence of lateral inhibitory interactions among orientation-selective neuronal populations in the primary visual cortex.
source: McTeague et al., 2015, using a generalization gradient of oriented gratings, explained their finding of visuocortical sharpening as a consequence of lateral inhibitory interactions among orientation-selective neuronal populations in the primary visual cortex.
evidence: This describes the interpretation from a previous study.

claim: Signals from frontoparietal attention networks may selectively facilitate CS+ representations in visual cortex, prompting local inhibitory interactions between adjacent cortical units.
source: In this case, signals from frontoparietal attention networks may selectively facilitate CS+ representations in visual cortex, prompting local inhibitory interactions between adjacent cortical units.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation.

claim: Top-down signals take the shape of a generalization gradient, and it is the organization of visual cortex that turns this gradient into a sharpening pattern through lateral inhibition.
source: In fact, ongoing computational modeling efforts in our laboratories explain these and other generalization data best by assuming that top-down signals take the shape of a generalization gradient (paralleling behavioral and autonomic data), and it is the organization of visual cortex that turns this gradient into a sharpening pattern through lateral inhibition.
evidence: This is based on ongoing computational modeling work.

claim: Sharpening would not be inherited by anterior areas but would result from the organization and geometry of visual cortical areas.
source: As such, sharpening would not be inherited by anterior areas but would result from the organization and geometry of visual cortical areas.
evidence: This is an inference from the computational modeling work.

claim: The orientation-tuning functions of visual neurons may be shaped by short-term plastic processes.
source: This interpretation is further supported by research demonstrating that the orientation-tuning functions of visual neurons may be shaped by short-term plastic processes (Dragoi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Inhibitory interactions may occur between similar faces along a gradient of morphs, in face-sensitive cortical areas.
source: Second, inhibitory interactions may occur between similar faces along a gradient of morphs, in face-sensitive cortical areas.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed in the discussion.

claim: Neuronal populations in face-sensitive cortical patches encode identity by combining their population tuning to sets of high-order shape and appearance dimensions.
source: This alternative hypothesis is in line with recent evidence suggesting that neuronal populations in face-sensitive cortical patches encode identity by combining their population tuning to sets of high-order shape and appearance dimensions (e.g. Chang and Tsao, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The results support the hypothesis that inhibitory interactions take place in extra-striate, higher order visuocortical areas.
source: Our results support the hypothesis that such interactions take place in extra-striate, higher order visuocortical areas, as we exploited the assets of high-density EEG recording and CSD-transformation leading to a precise topographical distribution of the ssVEP signal.
evidence: This is an inference from the topographical distribution of the ssVEP signal.

claim: The signal topographies reveal right-lateralized activation peaks for the signal-to-noise ratios of the ssVEP signal.
source: These signal topographies reveal indeed right-lateralized activation peaks for the signal-to-noise ratios of the ssVEP signal (Figure 4) as well as for the model fit of the lateral inhibition pattern (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the topographical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The results are compatible with the idea of a right-hemispheric dominance of face perception.
source: Thus, our results are compatible with the idea of a right-hemispheric dominance of face perception (Rossion, 2014) and suggest an involvement of the right OFA or FFA in sharpening face discrimination on the basis of lateral inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference from the right-lateralized activation pattern, supported by a citation.

claim: The results suggest an involvement of the right OFA or FFA in sharpening face discrimination on the basis of lateral inhibition.
source: Thus, our results are compatible with the idea of a right-hemispheric dominance of face perception (Rossion, 2014) and suggest an involvement of the right OFA or FFA in sharpening face discrimination on the basis of lateral inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference from the topographical findings.

claim: Visuocortical system engagement is associated with self-reported symptoms of social anxiety.
source: Furthermore, Bayesian model and correlational analyses revealed that visuocortical system engagement is associated with self-reported symptoms of social anxiety.
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian and correlational analyses.

claim: Cortical engagement in response to threat-associated phobic-relevant stimuli is dimensionally related to social anxiety.
source: Here, we provide further evidence that cortical engagement in response to threat-associated phobic-relevant stimuli is dimensionally related to social anxiety.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: No association was found between strength of social anxiety and (over)generalization of conditioned fear in terms of higher fear responses (efferent system) to the generalization stimuli.
source: It is important to mention, however, that we - replicating Ahrens et al., 2016 – found no association between strength of social anxiety and (over)generalization of conditioned fear in terms of a higher fear responses (efferent system) to the generalization stimuli.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, replicating previous work.

claim: Social anxiety was associated with a more pronounced lateral inhibition pattern in visuocortical responses to generalization stimuli.
source: Instead, we observed social anxiety to be associated with a more pronounced lateral inhibition pattern in visuocortical responses to generalization stimuli.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: The effect of social anxiety on visuocortical responses was only evident in the Bayesian-analysis but not in the corresponding ANOVA.
source: Please note that the effect of social anxiety on visuocortical responses was only evident in the Bayesian-analysis but not in the corresponding ANOVA.
evidence: This is a methodological observation about the statistical analyses.

claim: The discrepancy between Bayesian and ANOVA results results from the differences regarding statistical power between omnibus- and contrast-analysis.
source: This discrepancy results from the differences regarding statistical power between omnibus- and contrast-analysis (Furr and Rosenthal, 2003).
evidence: This is an explanation supported by a citation.

claim: Social anxiety was not associated with visuocortical responses for the quadratic or linear trend model, but only for the lateral inhibition model.
source: This notion is substantiated by the finding that social anxiety was not associated with visuocortical responses for the quadratic or linear trend model, but only for the lateral inhibition model.
evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian model comparison.

claim: There was no substantial increase in differential ssVEP-SNRs (CS+ vs CS-) from habituation to acquisition.
source: One important limitation to our findings is that there was no substantial increase in differential ssVEP-SNRs (CS+ vs CS-) from habituation to acquisition, t(66) = 0.83, p = 0.409, d = 0.10, CI95 = [−0.14, 0.34].
evidence: This is a finding from a cross-phase comparison.

claim: Cross-phase comparisons confound any conditioning effects with time-dependent effects such as adaptation.
source: However, this seems unlikely in our study, because the mapping of the two faces to the CS+ and CS- was fully counterbalanced between subjects. In addition, in the differential conditioning literature, cross-phase comparisons are typically avoided because they confound any conditioning effects with time-dependent effects such as adaptation, in which both the CS+ and CS- evoked responses decline over time, from habituation to acquisition and finally into the extinction phase.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the conditioning literature.

claim: The acquisition data provided substantial evidence for the notion that fear conditioning selectively amplifies the CS+ evoked ssVEP above and beyond the differences present during habituation.
source: This analysis yielded a BF (posterior odds over prior odds) of 4.77, error = 1.3%, suggesting that the acquisition data provided substantial evidence for the notion that fear conditioning selectively amplifies the CS+ evoked ssVEP above and beyond the differences present during habituation.
evidence: This is a finding from the post-hoc Bayesian analysis.

claim: The study extends current notions of generalization learning by demonstrating the involvement of inhibitory interactions among feature-specific neurons in the visuocortical system during fear generalization to facial stimuli.
source: In conclusion, our study extends current notions of generalization learning, by demonstrating the involvement of inhibitory interactions among feature-specific neurons in the visuocortical system during fear generalization to facial stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's contribution.

claim: Subjects were 67 undergraduate students with normal or corrected vision and without past or present psychiatric diagnosis or family history of epilepsy.
source: Subjects were 67 undergraduate students (age: M = 24.10, SD = 6.33; 48 female) with normal or corrected vision and without past or present psychiatric diagnosis or family history of epilepsy (self-report), who were paid or received course credit for participation.
evidence: This describes the participant characteristics.

claim: The sample size was based on the effect sizes of previous aversive conditioning studies using ssVEPs and adapted for covariate-analyses.
source: The sample size was based on the effect sizes of previous aversive conditioning studies using ssVEPs (McTeague et al., 2015; Miskovic and Keil, 2013) and adapted for covariate-analyses.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the sample size.

claim: Conditioned stimuli consisted of two pictures of female actresses with a neutral facial expression taken from the NimStim Set of Facial Expressions.
source: Conditioned stimuli (CS) consisted of two pictures of female actresses with a neutral facial expression taken from the NimStim Set of Facial Expressions (Tottenham et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the stimuli used in the study.

claim: Pictures were shown on a 17-inch monitor in a flickering mode at a frequency of 12 Hz in order to elicit ssVEPs.
source: Pictures were shown on a gray background on a 17-inch monitor (resolution = 1,280×1,024 pixel) in a flickering mode at a frequency of 12 Hz in order to elicit ssVEPs.
evidence: This describes the stimulus presentation method.

claim: The US consisted of the respective CS+ face displaying a fearful expression and a simultaneously presented 95 dB shrill female scream.
source: The US consisted of the respective CS+ face displaying a fearful expression and a simultaneously presented 95 dB shrill female scream of the IADS (Bradley and Lang, 1999).
evidence: This describes the unconditioned stimulus used in the study.

claim: Four generalization stimuli were created by morphing the two faces in 20% steps.
source: Four generalization stimuli (GS) were created by morphing the two faces in 20% steps using a face-morphing software (Squirlz Morph; Xiberpix, Solihull, UK).
evidence: This describes how the generalization stimuli were created.

claim: The experiment comprised three blocks: habituation, acquisition, and generalization.
source: The experiment comprised three blocks (habituation, acquisition, generalization).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: During acquisition, one of the faces (CS+) was paired in 12 of 15 trials (80% reinforcement) with the US.
source: During acquisition, one of the faces (CS+) was paired in 12 of 15 trials (80% reinforcement) with the US, which lasted 1500 ms and was presented at the offset of the CS+ with a sound volume of 95 dB by Labtech speakers (Labtech International Ltd., Ringmer, East Sussex, GB) and a Kenwood KA-3010-Amplifier (Kenwood Electronics, Heusenstamm, GER).
evidence: This describes the conditioning procedure.

claim: During generalization, 6 of the 15 CS+ were still followed by the US to prevent early extinction (40% reinforcement).
source: While CS- and GS were never reinforced, 6 of the 15 CS+ were still followed by the US to prevent early extinction (40% reinforcement, Lissek et al., 2008) (see Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the generalization procedure.

claim: Electrocortical activity was measured via 129 electrodes using an Electrical Geodesics high-density EEG System.
source: Electrocortical activity was measured via 129 electrodes using an Electrical Geodesics (EGI, Eugene, OR) high-density EEG System referenced to Cz, recorded with a sampling rate of 250 Hz and online bandpass filtered with 0.1 and 100 Hz and a 50 Hz notch filter.
evidence: This describes the EEG recording setup.

claim: Current source densities were calculated to increase spatial resolution of the EEG signal.
source: To increase spatial resolution of the EEG signal, we then calculated the current source densities (CSD) of the time-averaged data.
evidence: This describes a data processing step.

claim: The CSD transformation offers the advantage of reducing the negative impact of volume conduction.
source: The CSD transformation offers the advantage of reducing the negative impact of volume conduction and thereby effectively minimizing unwanted topographical variability between subjects by quantifying source densities (Junghöfer et al., 1997; Kayser and Tenke, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to methodological work.

claim: The signal-to-noise ratio is a unitless measure that accounts for both the evoked signal and the random noise in the data.
source: The SNR is a unitless measure that accounts for both the evoked signal and the random noise in the data and has recently been used in other ssVEP paradigms as well (Barry-Anwar et al., 2018; Boylan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to previous studies.
